title: The sheep and the goats (Matthew 25:31–46)
hook: the king says: when you fed the hungry and visited the prisoner, you did it to me

segments.voice: Yesterday, ten bridesmaids, virgins in the old telling, waited for a midnight groom; only five had spare oil.

A king sits on his throne, and all the nations of the world gather before him. He separates them, the way a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. To the ones on his right he says: come in. When I was hungry, you fed me. When I was thirsty, you gave me a drink. I was a stranger, and you took me in. I had no clothes, and you clothed me. I was sick, and you visited me. I was in prison, and you came to me. And the people on his right are baffled. When? When did we ever see you hungry? It's the last story Jesus tells in Matthew's Gospel before the plot against him begins.
screen: `A KING ON A THRONE.` → `I WAS HUNGRY, AND YOU FED ME.` → `WHEN DID WE SEE YOU?`

segments.voice: The king's answer: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." Here's what makes it strange: neither group knew. The helpers thought they were just feeding a hungry man. The ones on the left, who walked past, ask the same question: when did we see you hungry and not help? They'd have helped, if they'd known. He had an ordinary face. The list is plain on purpose. No miracles. Things anyone could do on a Tuesday. Catholic tradition took this list, added burying the dead, and called them the corporal works of mercy, the works of the body. Christian hospitals, food banks and prison ministries often point back to this passage. Who are the least of these? Christians have read it two ways: everyone in need, anywhere, or Jesus's own followers who are poor and suffering. Both readings have their defenders, and in both, the king is found in the one who needs help. It's a hard story too: the ones who walked past are sent away, and Matthew doesn't soften it. And with this, the parables end. Fifteen days of stories: seeds and yeast, a lost sheep, a lost coin, a pearl, workers paid too much, buried talents, bigger barns, a servant who wouldn't forgive, two men praying, a widow knocking, an empty banquet, a flask of oil. And last, a king with an ordinary face.
screen: `NEITHER GROUP KNEW` · `A LIST ANYONE CAN DO` · `WHO ARE THE LEAST OF THESE?` · `THE LAST OF THE PARABLES` · then, large: `YE HAVE DONE IT UNTO ME.`

segments.voice: Go down the king's list slowly, one breath each: hungry, thirsty, a stranger, without enough to wear, sick, in prison. With each one, let a face come, if one does, someone real, someone you've walked past or someone you know. Then choose one person you could feed, visit or clothe this week, and hold that plan as you sit.
Least. The smallest, the easiest to overlook: whatever you did for the least, you did for me.
Your line: he wears ordinary faces. Tomorrow the stories go back to the beginning: a small town called Nazareth, and a young woman named Mary.

howItsDone: Christians put this passage into practice through food banks, prison visiting, hospital chaplaincy and clothing drives, and Catholics count its acts among the corporal works of mercy.
